title: Rejoicing in praise
hookLine: be glad when others are praised, not jealous (Bodhicaryavatara 6)
tomorrow: if effort isn't grinding, what is it?

lines: WHY DOES IT FEEL LIKE A LOSS?
cards: The group chat lights up. Someone has posted the list for the spring show, and there's a friend's name in the spot you quietly hoped would be yours. Hearts stack up under it.
Your thumb hovers. You could add a heart. You could type congrats with a single period, which everyone can read.
Or you could put the phone face down and let your stomach do the thing. Nobody cheated. Nobody wronged you.
So why does someone else's good news land like a small loss?

teach.b: Shantideva noticed that exact sting. In his chapter on patience, kshanti, he turns from enemies to something quieter: envy. Someone else is being praised, and he asks his own mind a question.
When people delight in praising someone, why don't you delight in it too? Then he pushes. The joy of rejoicing costs nothing and harms nobody; he calls it a pleasure without fault.
And then the turn that makes it his.
You said you wanted every being to be happy, even to wake up. Now one of them gets a little praise, and you're upset? Their gladness is the very thing you wished for.
Buddhists have a word for this move: anumodana, rejoicing, being glad at another's good. Envy treats praise like a pie, as if their slice came out of yours.
Shantideva's answer is plainer: their praise was never yours to lose. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't pretend the sting isn't there.
He questions it, the way you'd question a friend who's being unfair to themselves. And there's a gift folded inside.
Rejoicing is a joy you can take in anyone's win, which means the supply of good news you get to enjoy just grew.

how: Rejoicing in the good of others is part of the daily practice of many Mahayana Buddhists, often recited alongside offering and confession; Shantideva's own guide includes a passage of rejoicing near its start.

o: accepting praise humbly, without enjoying it
being glad when someone else gets the praise
praising yourself so that others will join in

games.q: envy and its answer — tap the pairs.
p: their slice came out of mine

s: Shantideva says a good practitioner never feels envy
he talks to his own envious mind and questions it; the sting comes first.
Shantideva calls the joy of rejoicing a pleasure without fault
it costs nothing and harms nobody, and it's open to anyone.
envy only shows up when someone has wronged you
in today's case nobody did anything wrong; that's what makes it hard.

games.q: your coworker gets thanked in a meeting for an idea you'd had too but never said out loud. by Shantideva's verses, what's the move?
o: be glad the idea is out in the world and add your thanks to hers.
mention afterward that you'd had it first, so the record is fair.
say nothing and wait until the sting passes before you speak to her.
games.why: Shantideva asks why we don't delight when others are praised. their gladness is what you'd wish them anyway, and rejoicing costs you nothing.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose good news stung a little, lately. Write them one honest line of praise, something true and specific about what they did well, and send it, or keep it ready to send.
If the words feel stiff, let them be stiff; the gladness can follow the words.

wordCard.voice: Rejoicing in praise: being glad when someone else is praised, instead of jealous. The Buddhist word is anumodana.

orig.note: Sanskrit: rejoicing, approval; being glad at another's good deeds.

carryVoice: Keep this: their praise is fine, and nothing of yours went missing. The patience chapter, closed.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 6.76-6.83 (why not delight when others are praised; a pleasure without fault; you wished all beings happy)
